classification.difficultyReason: Order each list, apply the taught odd- or even-sized median-of-halves rule, average central pairs where needed, and subtract to obtain range and IQR. The choice of positions is routine and explicitly taught.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess interquartile range from numerical lists, with range as a supporting summary statistic.
questions.methodNote: Order the data. For odd-sized sets omit the median before splitting into equal halves; for even-sized sets split directly into equal halves. Find the median of each half, averaging its middle two values where necessary. Calculate range as maximum minus minimum and IQR as Q3 minus Q1. Example 2 on PDF page 4 is the printed reference.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Order each list, apply the taught odd- or even-sized median-of-halves rule, average central pairs where needed, and subtract to obtain range and IQR. The choice of positions is routine and explicitly taught.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied keys to read the ordered plots, count positions for the median and each half's median, and subtract the quartiles. Part a requires averaging pairs for both quartiles, but the displayed example directly supplies the method.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts assess quartiles and median from a stem-and-leaf display, followed by the interquartile range.
questions.methodNote: Order values, locate the median, divide into equal lower and upper halves, and find each half's median. Exclude the middle value for odd-sized datasets. Calculate IQR as Q3 minus Q1. Example 3 demonstrates reading positions directly from a stem-and-leaf plot.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the supplied keys to read the ordered plots, count positions for the median and each half's median, and subtract the quartiles. Part a requires averaging pairs for both quartiles, but the displayed example directly supplies the method.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate frequencies into a weighted total and cumulative positions, then locate the median and quartiles; these are routine linked procedures.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied frequencies determine repeated ordered values and their weighted sum. The task principally assesses summary statistics from a frequency table, with quartile subtraction also directly assessed. Mode prerequisite evidence remains missing.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–5 locate medians in ordered data, split the data into equal halves, find the median of each half and subtract the quartiles. Page 16 teaches the frequency-weighted mean. None of the supplied teaching pages explicitly teaches finding the mode from a frequency table.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate frequencies into a weighted total and cumulative positions, then locate the median and quartiles; these are routine linked procedures.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the median-of-halves method to positions rather than values, distinguishing whether the central observation is excluded and locating each half's middle pair.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 applies the taught median-of-halves convention to positions rather than observed values, so five-number-summary is the closest existing skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 gives the median position as (n+1)/2. Pages 3–4 divide ordered data into equal halves, omitting the median for odd sample sizes, and take each half's median for its quartile. Page 5 reinforces the positional method; page 16 concerns means and is not needed here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the median-of-halves method to positions rather than values, distinguishing whether the central observation is excluded and locating each half's middle pair.

classification.difficultyReason: Decode the already ordered stem-and-leaf plot, count to the middle pairs of the whole set and its halves, and subtract the quartiles.

questions.mappingNote: Part a reads the extreme heights and subtracts them. Part b averages positions 10 and 11. Part c finds the medians of the two 10-value halves, then subtracts the quartiles. Determining the IQR is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–4 explain ordering values, averaging the two middle values for even-sized sets, dividing the data into equal halves and subtracting the lower quartile from the upper quartile. Page 5 Example 3 applies median and quartile positions directly to a stem-and-leaf plot; its measures-of-spread summary defines range and IQR. Page 16 concerns means and is unnecessary for this question.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Decode the already ordered stem-and-leaf plot, count to the middle pairs of the whole set and its halves, and subtract the quartiles.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that the leaves are unsorted, order values within each stem, then exclude the central observation and find the two half-medians before subtracting.

questions.mappingNote: This question directly assesses IQR from a decimal stem-and-leaf display. Its unsorted leaves must be ordered before applying the taught method.
questions.methodNote: Arrange values in ascending order, omit the median for an odd-sized dataset, find the median of each remaining half, then subtract the lower quartile from the upper quartile. Page 5 Example 3 applies quartiles to a stem-and-leaf display.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that the leaves are unsorted, order values within each stem, then exclude the central observation and find the two half-medians before subtracting.

classification.difficultyReason: Order the expenditures, exclude the seventh value, and average the middle pair of each six-value half; part b directly uses those quartiles.

questions.mappingNote: Question 7 applies these methods to 13 weekly expenditures. The two halves each contain six values, requiring the middle-pair averaging method. Page 16 was inspected but its mean methods are not needed.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–5 teach ordering data, locating the median, excluding it for an odd-sized dataset, taking the median of each half and calculating IQR as upper quartile minus lower quartile. Page 4 also demonstrates averaging the middle pair in an even-sized group.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Order the expenditures, exclude the seventh value, and average the middle pair of each six-value half; part b directly uses those quartiles.

classification.difficultyReason: Reverse the summary process to fix five positions in an ordered seven-value list, then choose two remaining entries within their ordering bounds to produce distinct valid sets.

questions.mappingNote: Applying the taught odd-sized-data method backwards fixes positions 1, 2, 4, 6 and 7; the two remaining positions allow distinct valid datasets.
questions.methodNote: Arrange values in numerical order, locate the middle value, exclude that median for an odd-sized dataset, and take the median of each remaining half to obtain the quartiles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reverse the summary process to fix five positions in an ordered seven-value list, then choose two remaining entries within their ordering bounds to produce distinct valid sets.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct counterexamples by controlling extreme values to move the mean beyond a quartile while preserving the relevant ordered positions, including a nonnegative example for the lower side.

questions.mappingNote: Constructing counterexamples requires comparing the mean with the quartiles; page 3 explains the influence of extreme values on the mean.
questions.methodNote: Order the values, omit the median for an odd-sized dataset, and take the medians of the two remaining halves. Calculate the mean by dividing the sum by the number of values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct counterexamples by controlling extreme values to move the mean beyond a quartile while preserving the relevant ordered positions, including a nonnegative example for the lower side.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose addition to recover the maximum from the range and subtraction to recover the lower quartile from the IQR; each part reverses a familiar difference definition.

questions.mappingNote: Part a reverses the range calculation to recover the maximum; part b reverses the interquartile-range calculation to recover Q1. Interquartile range is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 5 defines range as highest minus lowest and interquartile range as upper quartile minus lower quartile. Pages 3–4 demonstrate calculating these differences and identify the quartiles as Q1 and Q3.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose addition to recover the maximum from the range and subtraction to recover the lower quartile from the IQR; each part reverses a familiar difference definition.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the two whisker endpoints as the extreme prices and read their values, interpolating the minimum between scale ticks.

questions.mappingNote: The question assesses reading two components of the five-number summary from a supplied boxplot.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 identifies the outer whisker endpoints as the minimum and maximum; read their values using the scale.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the two whisker endpoints as the extreme prices and read their values, interpolating the minimum between scale ticks.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the appropriate endpoints, median line and box edges, subtract for range and IQR, and interpret the scale in thousands of dollars.

questions.mappingNote: The question reads minimum and median from a boxplot and calculates range and IQR. Interquartile range is the most advanced directly assessed calculation.
questions.methodNote: Pages 3–4 define range and interquartile range as maximum minus minimum and upper quartile minus lower quartile. Page 7 identifies the endpoints, box edges and median line of a boxplot and demonstrates calculating the IQR.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select the appropriate endpoints, median line and box edges, subtract for range and IQR, and interpret the scale in thousands of dollars.

classification.difficultyReason: Read the minimum and median, interpolate values between labelled ticks, and apply the standard endpoint and quartile differences for range and IQR.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–b read the minimum and median; parts c–d calculate spreads from the displayed endpoints and quartiles. IQR is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 3–4 define the range and IQR as maximum minus minimum and upper quartile minus lower quartile. Page 7 identifies the whisker endpoints, box edges and internal median line in a boxplot.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read the minimum and median, interpolate values between labelled ticks, and apply the standard endpoint and quartile differences for range and IQR.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the stem-and-leaf display, locate the median and quartiles by ordered positions, then choose a scale and translate the five-number summary into a boxplot without intermediate prompts.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed task is construction of a boxplot; finding the five-number summary supports that construction.
questions.methodNote: Split ordered data into equal halves, take each half's median for the quartiles, and draw a boxplot showing the minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and maximum on a numerical scale, as in Example 4.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret the stem-and-leaf display, locate the median and quartiles by ordered positions, then choose a scale and translate the five-number summary into a boxplot without intermediate prompts.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the central observation, exclude it when finding the two half-medians, calculate IQR and transfer the five-number summary to a labelled boxplot. These are explicitly scaffolded routine linked procedures.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies the median-of-halves method to 21 ordered observations. Part b directly applies Example 4's boxplot construction, making box-plots the most advanced assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 3–4 find quartiles as the medians of the lower and upper halves, omitting the overall median for an odd-sized dataset. Page 7, Example 4, calculates quartiles and IQR before drawing a boxplot from the five-number summary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Exclude the central observation when splitting the ordered data, average the middle values of each half, calculate IQR and use these scaffolded results to construct a scaled boxplot.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught division of data into quarters to identify the proportions below the median and lower quartile, inside the box and in each whisker.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts assess approximate proportions represented by regions of a boxplot, directly matching box-plot-percentages.
questions.methodNote: Pages 3–4 explain quartiles as quarters of ordered data and the interquartile range as the spread of the middle 50%. Page 7 identifies the median, quartiles, box and whiskers, explicitly stating that the box represents the middle 50%.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the taught division of data into quarters to identify the proportions below the median and lower quartile, inside the box and in each whisker.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that the two outer quartile intervals can have equal numerical spans, so unequal whisker lengths are not compulsory; only a yes-or-no response is requested.

questions.mappingNote: The closest catalogue skill is box-plots: this question checks understanding of the components of a boxplot rather than calculating proportions or comparing datasets.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 defines whiskers as the horizontal lines from the lower and upper quartiles to the minimum and maximum. Their lengths represent numerical distances, which can be equal. Pages 3–4 establish the quartile definitions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that the two outer quartile intervals can have equal numerical spans, so unequal whisker lengths are not compulsory; only a yes-or-no response is requested.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect quartiles dividing observations into equal proportions with unequal numerical spreads to explain why the median can lie off-centre.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 tests the distinction between equal proportions of observations and equal numerical distances on a boxplot.
questions.methodNote: Interpret the box as the middle 50% of the data, bounded by the lower and upper quartiles, with the median marked inside it.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect quartiles dividing observations into equal proportions with unequal numerical spreads to explain why the median can lie off-centre.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the graphical feature representing each named statistic and directly compare positions or widths on the supplied common scale.

questions.mappingNote: Question 9 directly applies the labelled boxplot definition and five-number-summary interpretation on page 7 to two related data sets.
questions.methodNote: Read the minimum and maximum from whisker endpoints, the quartiles from box edges and the median from the interior line. Compare range and interquartile range using their spans on a common scale.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the graphical feature representing each named statistic and directly compare positions or widths on the supplied common scale.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the preceding comparisons to justify overall class performance, weighing Class A's higher typical marks against Class B's higher individual maximum.

questions.mappingNote: Question 10 applies the five-number-summary interpretation and comparison of related datasets explicitly introduced on page 7.
questions.methodNote: Read the minimum and maximum at the whisker ends, the quartiles at the box edges and the median at the line inside the box. Compare box widths for interquartile ranges.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the preceding comparisons to justify overall class performance, weighing Class A's higher typical marks against Class B's higher individual maximum.

classification.difficultyReason: After reading summaries and applying supplied ranking criteria, devise a different defensible criterion that favours C, such as the highest minimum rating.

questions.mappingNote: Question 11 applies the labelled boxplot and five-number-summary interpretation taught on page 7 to three related datasets and alternative ranking criteria.
questions.methodNote: Identify the minimum and maximum at whisker endpoints, quartiles at the box edges and median at the internal line. Compare interquartile ranges using upper quartile minus lower quartile.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: After reading summaries and applying supplied ranking criteria, devise a different defensible criterion that favours C, such as the highest minimum rating.

classification.difficultyReason: Links the scaffolded quartile and IQR calculations to the taught outlier test, then selects non-outlying endpoints and represents the summary as a boxplot.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b use the quartile procedure on pages 3–4. Part c applies the explicit outlier and whisker rules on page 10 and the worked constructions on pages 11 and 13.
questions.methodNote: Order the values, find the median, omit it for odd-sized data and find the medians of the two halves. Calculate IQR as Q3 minus Q1. Identify outliers beyond Q1 minus 1.5 IQR or Q3 plus 1.5 IQR; whiskers end at the most extreme non-outlying observations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Links the scaffolded quartile and IQR calculations to the taught outlier test, then selects non-outlying endpoints and represents the summary as a boxplot.

classification.difficultyReason: Uses the prompted quartiles and IQR to identify outliers, distinguish them from whisker endpoints and construct a suitably scaled boxplot; the large income values add arithmetic rather than conceptual demand.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 explicitly references Example 7. Pages 3–4 establish quartiles; pages 10–11 establish the outlier rule and whisker endpoints; page 13 illustrates this construction.
questions.methodNote: Order the data; take the median of each half for quartiles. Calculate IQR, apply strict 1.5 IQR outlier boundaries and end whiskers at the extreme non-outlier observations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses the prompted quartiles and IQR to identify outliers, distinguish them from whisker endpoints and construct a suitably scaled boxplot; the large income values add arithmetic rather than conceptual demand.

classification.difficultyReason: Interprets histogram tail direction and symmetry, then connects these features to box position, whisker lengths and outlier placement to match the displays and name each distribution shape.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is identifying distribution shape from histograms and boxplots; quartile calculations are not requested.
questions.methodNote: Identify symmetry or skew from histogram tails; compare the box location, relative whisker lengths and side of outliers. Page 10 defines the three distribution shapes, page 11 demonstrates positive skew, and page 13 demonstrates symmetry.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interprets histogram tail direction and symmetry, then connects these features to box position, whisker lengths and outlier placement to match the displays and name each distribution shape.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate stem-and-leaf data into equal-width histogram classes and a quartile-based boxplot, then compare tails to infer skewness. The familiar representations and procedures are explicitly requested.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 requires reading the supplied stem-and-leaf display, constructing a histogram and boxplot, calculating quartiles and IQR, and using tail lengths to describe shape. The supplied reuse candidates have different datasets and tasks, so neither is source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Pages 3–4 teach ordered-data quartiles, omitting the median for an odd number of observations, and IQR as Q3 minus Q1. Pages 10–11 teach outlier fences, whiskers ending at the extreme non-outliers, histogram classes and shape comparisons. Page 13 supplies a complete histogram/boxplot comparison.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate the ordered stem-and-leaf data into histogram classes and a quartile-based boxplot, then identify negative skew from the lower tails. The representations are linked through familiar, explicitly requested procedures.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied quartiles to calculate the IQR and both outlier fences, then compare each candidate with those bounds. This is a short routine chain with no need to organise data or choose a method.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses the formal IQR outlier rule using the same supplied quartiles. Neither reuse candidate matches this complete source task.
questions.methodNote: Pages 3–4 define IQR as the upper quartile minus the lower quartile. Page 10 defines outliers as values below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. Example 5 on pages 10–11 demonstrates calculating these limits; Example 7 on page 13 reinforces outlier identification.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the supplied quartiles to calculate the IQR and both outlier fences, then compare each candidate with those bounds. This is a short routine chain with no need to organise data or choose a method.

classification.difficultyReason: Organise the observations into an ordered stem-and-leaf display, use that ordering to obtain quartiles and check boxplot whiskers, then recognise approximate symmetry from similar spreads on either side.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) organises the same raw dataset; part (b) directly assesses boxplot construction using quartiles and the outlier rule; part (c) interprets distribution shape. The supplied reuse candidates have different datasets and tasks and are not source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Pages 3–4 teach ordering the data and taking medians of the two halves. Pages 10–11 teach the 1.5 IQR outlier boundaries and whiskers ending at the extreme non-outliers. Page 13 relates approximate symmetry to the boxplot's whisker lengths. Explicit prerequisite teaching for constructing a stem-and-leaf diagram is absent from the supplied evidence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Organise the observations into an ordered stem-and-leaf display, use that ordering to obtain quartiles and check boxplot whiskers, then recognise approximate symmetry from similar spreads on either side.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate the explicitly requested quartiles and IQR from ordered observations, apply the taught fences, and distinguish the upper non-outlier whisker endpoint from the separately marked value 62.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) applies the median-of-halves method; part (b) constructs the taught modified boxplot; part (c) formally tests observations against the IQR fences. The directly assessed outlier rule supports the primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 3–4 teach ordering data, splitting even-sized data into equal halves, averaging middle values and calculating Q3−Q1. Pages 10–11 define the 1.5 IQR outlier rule and whiskers ending at extreme non-outlier observations. Page 13 demonstrates a boxplot with separate outlier markers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate the explicitly requested quartiles and IQR from ordered observations, apply the taught fences, and distinguish the upper non-outlier whisker endpoint from the separately marked value 62.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a repeated-value dotplot, compute quartiles and fences for a modified boxplot, select the extreme non-outliers as whisker endpoints and interpret the long upper tail. This is routine linked representation and interpretation.

questions.mappingNote: The whole task combines dotplot representation, a modified boxplot and shape interpretation. Boxplot construction is the primary skill; the outlier rule and skewness are directly assessed through the required displays and comment.
questions.methodNote: Pages 3–4 teach ordered data, the median of each half and IQR. Pages 10–11 teach the 1.5 IQR outlier rule, whiskers ending at the extreme non-outlying observations and positive skew. Page 13 demonstrates a completed modified boxplot. No supplied teaching page explicitly teaches dotplot construction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent repeated observations in a dotplot, derive quartiles and outlier fences for a modified boxplot, and interpret the longer upper tail. Choosing the largest non-outlier as the whisker endpoint is the key routine decision.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught mean formula to the supplied kicks, count the observations and round; no method selection or interpretation is needed.

questions.mappingNote: This question directly assesses the mean of an ungrouped list; no standard deviation or frequency-table method is required.
questions.methodNote: Page 16 defines the mean as the sum of the values divided by their number. Example 8 substitutes the complete list into a fraction and rounds the result to two decimal places.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the taught mean formula to the supplied kicks, count the observations and round; no method selection or interpretation is needed.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate each city's mean using the same direct procedure, then identify the larger result in context.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses calculating and comparing arithmetic means of two raw datasets.
questions.methodNote: Use the mean formula and Example 8: add all observations, divide by the number of observations, and round the final result to two decimal places.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate each city's mean using the same direct procedure, then identify the larger result in context.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that the original total must be recovered as five times the mean, then add the new mass and divide by the updated count.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed task is calculating the effect of adding a value on the mean; the source mean definition and Example 8 support the arithmetic method.
questions.methodNote: Use mean = sum of values divided by number of values. Recover the initial sum by multiplying the mean by the number of masses, then add the new mass and divide by six.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that the original total must be recovered as five times the mean, then add the new mass and divide by the updated count.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert each group mean into total marks using its test count, then combine totals and divide by ten rather than averaging the two means equally.

questions.mappingNote: The question assesses calculating a combined mean from unequal group sizes; the mean calculation skill is the closest supplied catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: Mean equals the sum of all values divided by their number. Recover each group total by multiplying its mean by its number of tests, then divide the combined total by ten.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert each group mean into total marks using its test count, then combine totals and divide by ten rather than averaging the two means equally.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate means and population standard deviations using the taught method, then explain that equal means can accompany different spreads by interpreting the larger standard deviation.

questions.mappingNote: Both data sets and their comparison directly assess calculation and interpretation of population standard deviation; calculating the mean is a prerequisite.
questions.methodNote: Find the mean, square the deviations from it, divide their sum by the number of observations, then take the square root. Example 10 supplies this method; page 19 specifies population standard deviation and explains that larger standard deviation means greater spread.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate means and population standard deviations using the taught method, then explain that equal means can accompany different spreads by interpreting the larger standard deviation.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied columns to calculate the frequency-weighted mean, then use that mean for deviations and weighted squares before dividing by total frequency and taking the square root.

questions.mappingNote: The requested extended frequency table directly assesses the taught population standard-deviation method, with frequency-table mean as a supporting skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 11 completes the frequency and product columns, calculates the mean, then completes deviations and frequency-weighted squared deviations. Divide their sum by total frequency and take the square root; use population standard deviation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the supplied columns to calculate the frequency-weighted mean, then use that mean for deviations and weighted squares before dividing by total frequency and taking the square root.

classification.difficultyReason: Enter each dataset into calculator statistics mode, select the taught population standard deviation and mean, and round the outputs; no comparison or explanation is required.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly require calculator means and population standard deviations, matching standard-deviation.
questions.methodNote: The mean is the sum divided by the number of values. Standard deviation uses the population divisor n. Page 19 explicitly recommends calculator statistics facilities and distinguishes population from sample standard deviation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Enter each dataset into calculator statistics mode, select the taught population standard deviation and mean, and round the outputs; no comparison or explanation is required.

classification.difficultyReason: Decode the stem-and-leaf values, apply the taught mean and population standard-deviation procedures, and use the calculated mean as a threshold for counting marks. These are routine linked steps with explicit prompts.

questions.mappingNote: The stem-and-leaf display supplies the dataset for all three parts; calculating population standard deviation is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Calculate the mean by dividing the total by the number of values. Standard deviation uses squared deviations divided by n, followed by a square root. Page 19 recommends calculator statistics for larger datasets and specifies population standard deviation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Decode the stem-and-leaf values, apply the taught mean and population standard-deviation procedures, and use the calculated mean as a threshold for counting marks. These are routine linked steps with explicit prompts.

classification.difficultyReason: Use frequencies as weights when calculating the mean and population standard deviation, then identify scores below the mean and total their frequencies. The main decision is interpreting frequencies consistently across familiar procedures.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced assessed operation is population standard deviation from a frequency table; part a also assesses the weighted mean.
questions.methodNote: Use the frequency-weighted mean and the population standard deviation, dividing the weighted sum of squared deviations by the total frequency. Page 19 recommends calculator statistics for non-integer means.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use frequencies as weights when calculating the mean and population standard deviation, then identify scores below the mean and total their frequencies. The main decision is interpreting frequencies consistently across familiar procedures.

classification.difficultyReason: Express deviations algebraically and connect their sum to the defining identity that the total equals the number of values times the mean. Generalising to an arbitrary data set requires symbolic reasoning, scaffolded by the three-value proof in part a.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts assess algebraic consequences of the arithmetic mean. The mean skill is the closest catalogue match; neither part requires calculating standard deviation.
questions.methodNote: Page 16 defines the mean as the sum divided by the number of values. Page 17 defines a deviation as a data value minus the mean and explicitly refers to Exercise 18D question 10 for the zero-sum proof. Page 18 reiterates that the sum of deviations is zero; page 19 retains the same mean and deviation notation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express deviations algebraically and connect their sum to the defining identity that the total equals the number of values times the mean. Generalising to an arbitrary data set requires symbolic reasoning, scaffolded by the three-value proof in part a.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate population standard deviations and compare datasets that share a mean, distinguishing centre from spread.

questions.mappingNote: Question 1 directly assesses population standard deviation and comparison of overall spread, rather than comparison of individual standardised scores. The supplied reuse candidates assess unrelated algebra and numerical indices and are not source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Pages 17–18 calculate the mean, square deviations, divide their sum by the number of data values and take the square root. Page 19 explicitly requires population standard deviation and explains that larger standard deviation means greater spread about the mean. Pages 22–23 develop interpretation and comparison using the mean and standard deviation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate population standard deviations and compare datasets that share a mean, distinguishing centre from spread.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate interval endpoints by adding and subtracting one or two given standard deviations.

questions.mappingNote: Each given mean and standard deviation determines two intervals. Calculating these endpoints is the closest directly assessed use of the standard-deviation skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 22 introduces intervals centred on the mean. Example 12 calculates their endpoints using the mean minus and plus one or two standard deviations. Its integer-score restriction does not apply to this question, which gives no discrete domain.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate interval endpoints by adding and subtracting one or two given standard deviations.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate population summary statistics and compare two marks by their distances from their respective means in standard deviations.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies population statistics to the two supplied lists. Part b directly follows Example 13, so comparing z-scores is the most advanced assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 17–18 calculate the mean and population standard deviation from squared deviations. Page 19 recommends calculator statistics for larger datasets and specifies division by n. Page 23, Example 13, compares test marks using their signed distances from their means measured in standard deviations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate population summary statistics and compare two marks by their distances from their respective means in standard deviations.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare each pair of marks by expressing their deviations from different means in standard deviation units.

questions.mappingNote: All four students require the relative-score comparison taught in Example 13. The supplied means and standard deviations eliminate any need to calculate summary statistics from raw data; compare-z-scores is the closest directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 17–19 define population standard deviation and its calculation. Page 22 interprets distances from the mean in standard deviation units. Page 23, Example 13, compares test marks by dividing each deviation from its respective mean by its standard deviation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare each pair of marks by expressing their deviations from different means in standard deviation units.

classification.difficultyReason: Read values and frequencies from three given bar charts, calculate population statistics, and apply taught translation and scaling rules. Later parts reuse the results and add familiar linked decisions.

questions.mappingNote: Parts b and c directly assess the effects of translating and scaling all data values; part a supplies their original statistics.
questions.methodNote: Use population standard deviation, dividing the sum of frequency-weighted squared deviations by total frequency. Compare spread about the mean and retain exact values until rounding.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read values and frequencies from bar charts, calculate population summary statistics, then apply taught translation and scaling rules to those results. These are routine linked procedures with the original statistics supplied by part a.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct maximally spread distributions by balancing values at opposite extremes, recognising that an unbalanced split shifts the mean. Part c additionally requires using only the minimum permitted middle values and balancing the remaining extremes.
